en: *Commentary on the Heart Sūtra of Prajñāpāramitā:
The Gate of Wondrous Joy*, composed by Mingkuang, disciple of [Master] Miaole.

Now, the Buddha-dharma is not remote; it is immediate within the mind. True Suchness (Tathatā) is not external; what could one seek by abandoning the body? It is only through delusion that one fails to see this.
Awakening lies within oneself; as soon as one resolves to attain it, one reaches clarity. It is not through faith in others or through cultivation that sudden realization occurs.

If one does not seek the medicine of the King of Physicians, when will one behold the light of the Great Sun? This brief commentary on the conditions for the practice of recitation and contemplation is provided as above;
a full exposition would exhaust an entire kalpa.
Regarding the title *Mahāprajñāpāramitāhṛdayasūtra*, there are briefly two distinctions based on the difference between the Sanskrit and Chinese languages:
*Mahāprajñāpāramitā* is the Sanskrit term, while *Hṛdayasūtra* is the Chinese term. If one were to preserve the full Sanskrit title, it could be stated as follows:
*Mahāprajñāpāramitāhṛdayasūtra*. If one were to preserve only the Chinese terminology, it could be called the *Sūtra on the Heart of Great Wisdom Reaching the Other Shore*.
Regarding the term *mahā*, according to the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, it has three meanings:
great (*mahat*), many (*bahu*), and superior (*viśiṣṭa*). Master Tiantai stated that "great" signifies the meaning of emptiness (*śūnyatā*), while "many" signifies...

The term "that which" refers to the superior meaning of the provisional, while "the one who" refers to the meaning within the middle; this is precisely the principle of the perfect fusion of the three truths, the True Suchness, and the Real Mark.
This is the principle that is the object of contemplation. As for "Prajñā," it refers to the wisdom that is the subject of contemplation;

this is the threefold Prajñā. The threefold Prajñā consists of the Prajñā of the Real Mark (*lakṣaṇa-prajñā*), the Prajñā of Contemplative Insight (*pratyavekṣaṇā-prajñā*), and the [Prajñā of] Textual Exposition (*dharma-paryāya-prajñā*).

*Śabdaprajñā* (letter-prajñā) is the wisdom of the principle within contemplation; *Lakṣaṇaprajñā* (reality-mark prajñā) is the wisdom that contemplates the principle of the Middle Truth (*madhyasatya*);
and *Pratyavekṣaṇaprajñā* (contemplative prajñā) is the wisdom that contemplates the principle of the Empty Truth (*śūnyasatya*).

These are called the "three wisdoms" according to their temporal designations. As for the "three contemplations," they refer to the contemplations of Emptiness (*śūnya*), the Provisional (*prajñapti*), and the Middle (*madhya*).
The "three knowledges" (*trividya*) refer to the knowledge of all things (*sarvajñatā*), the knowledge of the paths (*mārgajñatā*), and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*).

"Pāramitā" carries the meaning of "reaching the other shore. Afflictions (*kleśa*) and birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) are called "this shore," while awakening (*bodhi*) and nirvana (*nirvāṇa*) are called "the other shore.
To realize that afflictions are themselves awakening and that birth-and-death is itself nirvana is what is meant by "that [shore]."
Delusion regarding enlightenment is called "this shore," while delusion regarding afflictions is called "nirvana" and "birth-and-death. What is termed "mind" refers to the essential and subtle mind;
it is precisely the principle of the three truths in perfect fusion discussed above. "Sūtra" refers to the teachings that expound these aforementioned meanings.

"Dharma" (法) means to instruct in the law and to instruct in constancy. Regarding the term "law" (法), its meaning is that of a guiding norm. [This applies to] all Buddhas of the three periods of time.

Because the Teacher attained Buddhahood by relying upon this, it is called "eternal"; for although the Buddhas of the three periods of time each appear in the world to preach, it is fundamentally eternal, without change or alteration.
As for the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara:
The person capable of such contemplation takes the single Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara as representative of all practitioners.
"When practicing the profound *prajñāpāramitā*... refers to this.
"Clearly understanding the principle that is contemplated" refers to the principle of the threefold truth in perfect fusion explained above.
"Illuminatively seeing that the five aggregates are all empty" clarifies the five aggregates that are the object of contemplation.

"Delivering from all suffering and calamity" means clearly contemplating that the five aggregates are all empty, thereby escaping all suffering and calamity. "Suffering" refers to the eight types of suffering:

the suffering of birth, the suffering of old age, the suffering of illness, the suffering of death, the suffering of separation from what one loves, the suffering of encountering what one hates, and the suffering of not obtaining what one seeks.
The five aggregates of clinging are suffering. As for the four calamities, they are: first, the calamity of desire; second, the calamity of existence; third, the calamity of views;
and fourth, the calamity of the flow of ignorance.
As for Śāriputra:
"To raise [the subject] and respond is to exalt the person.
"Form is not different from emptiness; emptiness is not different from form; form is itself emptiness;

emptiness is itself form" clarifies the principle of the perfect fusion of the three truths (*trisatya*). That "form is itself emptiness" does not mean that form is extinguished to become emptiness. That "emptiness... [is itself form...]
"This form is not separate from emptiness; this form is also what is called the Middle Truth. It is said that it is emptiness, it is the provisional, and it is the middle.
Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are also like this."

This can be understood by analogy with the aforementioned aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*). Among these five aggregates, the first, the aggregate of form, is the body; the remaining four aggregates are the mind (*citta*).
That which is called "form" refers to phenomena that possess physical shape and resistance; that which is called "mind" refers to phenomena that are formless and non-resistant.
When one speaks of "form" and "mind," form and mind are not two distinct dharmas. Why? Because the mind does not exist [apart from form].
Because it is neither internal nor external nor intermediate, but pervades all places like empty space.
"Śāriputra" refers to the person who was raised as the interlocutor.
Regarding the statement that "all these dharmas have the characteristic of emptiness—neither arising nor ceasing, neither defiled nor pure, neither increasing nor decreasing":
what is this? It is the nature of the mind, which is intrinsically pure, empty, and quiescent, yet fully possesses the three thousand realms and hundred worlds of all dharmas.
This "intrinsic emptiness and quiescence" refers to the principle of the Truth of Emptiness (*śūnyatā-satya*); although its nature is quiescent, it fully possesses the three thousand realms.

The "thousand dharmas" are the principle of the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*). That which is neither empty nor conventional and is inconceivable is the principle of the middle truth (*madhyama-satya*).
These three principles of truth exist as impurity in the Buddha but as non-defilement in ordinary beings; they exist as non-arising in the Buddha but as non-extinction in ordinary beings;
they exist as non-increase in the Buddha but as non-decrease in ordinary beings.
"Therefore, in emptiness there is no form, no sensation, perception, mental formations, or consciousness.
This concludes the explanation of the meaning of the five aggregates. The above exposition on the five aggregates is taught for those of superior faculties.
"Having no eye, ear, nose, tongue, body,
or mind" clarifies the absence of the six internal sense bases (*ṣaḍ-āyatana*).
"Having no form, sound, odor, taste, touch, or mental object" [clarifies the absence of the six external sense bases].
To clarify that there are no external six sense-objects (*ṣaḍ-viṣaya*) is also to clarify that the twelve bases (*dvādaśāyatana*) are empty. "Base" (*āyatana*) has the meaning of "entering";
it refers to the six faculties entering into the six objects. Regarding the forms encountered by the eye, there are three kinds:
attractive forms, unattractive forms, and neutral forms. Regarding the sounds encountered by the ear, there are likewise three kinds of sounds.
That is to say, there are three kinds of sounds perceived by the ear: pleasant sounds, unpleasant sounds, and neutral sounds.
There are three kinds of odors perceived by the nose: pleasant odors, unpleasant odors, and neutral odors. There are also three kinds of tastes perceived by the tongue:
pleasant tastes, unpleasant tastes, and neutral tastes. [There are likewise three kinds of tangibles] perceived by the body...
Contact (*sparśa*) is also of three kinds: agreeable contact, disagreeable contact, and neutral contact. The mental objects (*dharma*) encountered by the mind are also of three kinds:
agreeable dharmas, disagreeable dharmas, and neutral dharmas. An agreeable form for the eye possesses both the cause of birth and death and the fruit of birth and death;
it is identical to the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*) and the Truth of Origination (*samudaya-satya*). Thus it is.
Thus, the eye-faculty possesses six afflictions; the same applies to the other five faculties. Altogether, the six faculties comprise thirty-six afflictions.

When categorized according to the three periods of time—past, present, and future—they total one hundred and eight afflictions. When categorized according to the three divisions of time—yesterday, today, and tomorrow—they likewise total one hundred and eight.
Furthermore, when categorized according to the three mental moments—preceding, middle, and succeeding thoughts—they likewise total one hundred and eight.
Furthermore, regarding the deluded mind, there are likewise one hundred and eight afflictions; regarding the awakened mind, it also possesses one hundred and eight samādhis. What are they?

When observing that the faculties and their objects are in mutual relation, the mind of mindfulness is immediately empty, immediate provisional, and immediate middle—this is simultaneously the possession of the Truths of Cessation and the Path.
The Truth of the Path is the cause of nirvana; the Truth of Cessation is the fruit of nirvana. The above constitutes the teaching for those of medium capacity.
It is said:
"There is no eye-element, and so on, up to no consciousness-element.
This clarifies that there are no eighteen elements, citing the first and the last for brevity. To speak in detail, [there are] the eye-element, the form-element, and the eye-...

The element of consciousness (*vijñāna-dhātu*), the element of the ear (*śrotra-dhātu*), the element of sound (*śabda-dhātu*), the element of ear-consciousness (*śrotra-vijñāna-dhātu*); the element of the nose (*ghrāṇa-dhātu*), the element of odor (*gandha-dhātu*), the element of nose-consciousness (*ghrāṇa-vijñāna-dhātu*);

the element of the tongue (*jihvā-dhātu*), the element of taste (*rasa-dhātu*), the element of tongue-consciousness (*jihvā-vijñāna-dhātu*); the element of the body (*kāya-dhātu*), the element of tangibility (*spraṣṭavya-dhātu*), the element of body-consciousness (*kāya-vijñāna-dhātu*); the element of the mind (*manas-dhātu*), the element of mental objects (*dharma-dhātu*), and the element of mind-consciousness (*mano-vijñāna-dhātu*). "Element" (*dhātu*) has the meaning of differentiation.
The six sense organs, the six objects, and the six consciousnesses together constitute the eighteen elements (*aṣṭādaśa-dhātavaḥ*). Thus it is concluded.
The above is explained for those of inferior faculties.

"There is no ignorance, nor is there the exhaustion of ignorance," and so on up to "there is no old age and death, nor is there the exhaustion of old age and death," refers to the twelve links of dependent origination in both forward and reverse order.
To speak of the forward order of the twelve links means that ignorance is the condition [for volitional formations].

Volitional formations (*saṃskāra*) depend on consciousness (*vijñāna*); consciousness depends on name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*); name-and-form depends on the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*); the six sense bases depend on contact (*sparśa*); contact depends on feeling (*vedanā*); feeling depends on craving (*tṛṣṇā*);
craving depends on clinging (*upādāna*); clinging depends on becoming (*bhava*); becoming depends on birth (*jāti*); and birth depends on aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and despair.

Regarding the reversal of the twelve links of dependent origination: when ignorance (*avidyā*) ceases, volitional formations cease; when volitional formations cease, consciousness ceases... [and so forth].
With the cessation of consciousness, name-and-form ceases; with the cessation of name-and-form, the six sense bases cease; with the cessation of the six sense bases, contact ceases;
with the cessation of contact, feeling ceases; with the cessation of feeling, craving ceases; with the cessation of craving, clinging ceases;

with the cessation of clinging, existence ceases; with the cessation of existence, birth ceases; and with the cessation of birth, old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and despair cease. Thus it is.
The twelve links of dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda) are of four kinds:

the twelve links of dependent origination with arising and ceasing, the twelve links of dependent origination without arising and ceasing, the immeasurable twelve links of dependent origination, and the unconditioned twelve links of dependent origination.
These are the principles elucidated by the four teachings. Among them, the twelve links of dependent origination with arising and ceasing refers to the Tripitaka Teaching, which is the lowest level.
The twelve links of dependent origination regarding birth and cessation as taught for the roots of the Śrāvakas is what is elucidated for those of middling capacity;
the twelve links of dependent origination regarding the immeasurable is what is elucidated for the Bodhisattvas of superior capacity according to the Separate Teaching (Pratyekabuddhas);
and the twelve links of dependent origination regarding non-activity is what is elucidated for the Bodhisattvas of the highest-superior capacity according to the Perfect Teaching.
The commentary also explains that the twelve links of dependent origination are categorized into three paths: the three links of ignorance, craving, and grasping constitute the path of afflictions;

the two links of volitional formations and existence constitute the path of karma; and the remaining seven links constitute the path of suffering. The path of suffering is transformed into the virtue of the *dharmakāya*;
the path of afflictions is transformed into the virtue of *prajñā*; and the path of karma is transformed into the virtue of liberation. (3)
The Path is also called the three obstructions, namely: the obstruction of retribution, the obstruction of afflictions, and the obstruction of karma.
"There is no suffering, origin, cessation, or path" clarifies the Four Noble Truths;
that is, it clarifies the causes and effects of birth-and-death and nirvana. The Truth of Suffering is the fruit of birth-and-death; the Truth of Origin...

The Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*) is the cause of birth and death; the Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*) is the fruit of *nirvāṇa*; and the Truth of the Path (*mārga-satya*) is the cause of *nirvāṇa*. Question:
For what reason is the fruit mentioned first and the cause mentioned later? Answer: Because one knows the cause by seeing the fruit. Regarding these Four Noble Truths, there are also four kinds:

the Four Truths of Arising and Ceasing (*utpāda-nirodha*), the Four Truths of Non-arising and Non-ceasing (*anutpāda-ananirodha*), the Four Truths of the Immeasurable (*apramāṇa*), and the Four Truths of the Unconditioned (*anabhisaṃskāra*).
The Truths are likewise the Fourfold Teachings and the Four Noble Truths.
Those who lack wisdom have no Bodhi.
Furthermore, there is no one who attains;
this means that there is no nirvana, for the true mark is a singular reality, and outside of this true mark there are no other dharmas.
Because there is nothing to be attained, the Bodhisattva, by relying on the Prajñāpāramitā, has a mind free from obstruction.
"Obstruction" means that because all bodhisattvas rely on prajñā and are without obstruction,
they have no fear; being far removed from all inverted dreams and delusions, they attain ultimate nirvāṇa.
This clarifies the attainment of benefit.
All Buddhas of the three periods of time, by relying on the *prajñāpāramitā*, have attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Regarding the statement that "one knows that because of Bodhi, the Prajñāpāramitā is a great divine mantra, a great illuminating mantra, an unsurpassed mantra, and an unequaled mantra":
this clarifies the principles of the four teachings. Specifically, "the great divine mantra" refers to the principle of the four truths of arising and ceasing within the Tripiṭaka Teaching.
"This is the Great Illuminating Mantra" refers to the principle of the Four Noble Truths of arising and ceasing according to the Shared Teaching;

"this is the Unsurpassed Mantra" refers to the principle of the immeasurable Four Noble Truths according to the Distinct Teaching; and "this is the Unequaled Mantra" refers to the principle of the unconditioned Four Noble Truths according to the Perfect Teaching.
"That which can eliminate all suffering is true and not false" clarifies the true principle of extracting from suffering and bestowing happiness; the above clearly reveals Prajñā.
Therefore, it is said that the mantra of the Prajñāpāramitā is as follows:
*gate gate pāragate pārasaṃgate bodhi svāhā*.
This above clarifies the secret Prajñā. Regarding *gate gate*: "gate" means "to go" and "to cross over"; this is the illumination.
*Pāra-gate* means "crossing over oneself"; *pārasaṃgate* means "crossing over both oneself and others" in general;
*bodhi* means "the state reached by both self and others together";
and *svāhā* means "the ultimate," signifying both the ultimate of phenomena (*dharmaparyanta*) and the ultimate of principle (*tattvaparyanta*). (And so forth.)
The Commentary on the Heart Sūtra (End).

Master Zhizhe internally realized the secret [teachings] while externally expounding the manifest teachings; Jingxi Yixing mutually served as teacher and disciple, transmitting and receiving the Perfect and Esoteric [teachings].
It was here at Shan River that [Yixing] entered the gate of Jingxi and produced this Commentary on the Heart Sūtra. This is the illumination.
The *Dainichi-e Kōmyō Kanzeon Shin-gyō Benken Benmitsu Jinbi Jinsen* (The Profound Practice of Avalokiteśvara:

Illuminating Wisdom of Mahāvairocana, Discerning the Exoteric and Esoteric, Exhaustively Beautiful and Perfect) is a work that fully elucidates the two types of karma established by the Mount Hiei school.

When this commentary was brought forth to manifest the transmission to Tōji during the era when the three mysteries were propagated, this preface was composed as a scriptural citation for the *Himitsu Ken* (Secret Key). Thus, students of the Tendai sect in the eastern capital must certainly rely upon it.

It is essential that one studies this; I look up to you with the wish that the Buddha-sun may increase in brilliance, that the True Dharma may abide for a long time, and that the sufferings and calamities of the myriad people across the four seas may be delivered so they reach the blissful shore of Mahāprajñāpāramitā. Thus it is said.
Engraved on the eighth day of the month of Yi-se (the seventh lunar month) in the second year of the Honghwa reign;
respectfully recorded by the resident monk Uimam of Eonungsa Temple in Rimmun Village, Amye-gun, Seji Province.
